overview:
Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa, home to more than 220 million people, about one in every six Africans. It faces the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, covers a little more land than Texas and Oklahoma together, and borders Benin, Niger, Chad, and Cameroon.

English is the official language, a shared tongue among speakers of more than 500 others; Hausa, Yoruba, and Igbo are the largest. Abuja, a planned city built in the middle of the country, became the capital in 1991, while Lagos on the coast is the biggest city in Africa and the engine of its business. Nigeria is a federal republic of 36 states with an elected president.

Nigeria pumps more oil than any other African country, but abroad it is just as well known for what it makes: Nollywood, one of the busiest film industries in the world, and Afrobeats music that fills playlists from Lagos to London.
landAndNature: Nigeria changes as you travel north. The coast is a maze of lagoons, sandbars, and the Niger Delta, where the river splits into hundreds of creeks through the largest mangrove forest in Africa. Behind it lies rainforest, then wide savanna across the middle belt, and finally dry Sahel near the Sahara, where Lake Chad has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s. The Jos Plateau rises cool in the center, and Chappal Waddi near the Cameroon border, at about 2,400 meters, is the highest point. Forest elephants, chimpanzees, and rare Cross River gorillas survive in the southeastern hills, the stocky drill monkey lives only here and in Cameroon, and hippos and manatees swim the delta creeks.
peopleAndCulture: Nigeria has as many cultures as languages. Yoruba towns hold masquerade festivals with towering costumed figures, the Igbo celebrate the new yam harvest each August, and Hausa emirates parade horsemen in a durbar at the end of Ramadan. Roughly half the country is Muslim and half Christian. The food is bold and spicy: jollof rice, whose recipe Nigerians and Ghanaians argue over endlessly, egusi soup thickened with melon seeds, pounded yam, and suya, skewered beef rubbed with peanut and pepper. Fela Kuti invented Afrobeat in the 1970s, and Chinua Achebe's novel Things Fall Apart is read worldwide. Soccer is a national obsession, and the Super Eagles have won three Africa Cup of Nations titles.
history: The Nok people were smelting iron and sculpting life-size terracotta heads more than 2,000 years ago. Later came the kingdoms of Ife and Benin, whose brass and bronze casting astonished European visitors, the Igbo communities of the southeast, and the Hausa city-states and Sokoto Caliphate of the north. From the 1500s this coast became a center of the transatlantic slave trade, and more than a million people were shipped away from its ports. Britain seized Lagos in 1861 and by 1914 governed the whole territory. Nigeria became independent on October 1, 1960. The Biafran civil war from 1967 to 1970 cost around a million lives, mostly from hunger. Military rule ended in 1999, and elections have been held since.
funFacts: Nollywood releases well over a thousand films a year, making Nigeria one of the world's largest film producers by number of titles.
More than 500 languages are spoken in Nigeria, more than in almost any other country on Earth.
The Benin Bronzes, taken by British forces in 1897, sit in museums around the world, and some have now been returned to Nigeria.
The town of Igbo-Ora calls itself the twin capital of the world, because twins are born there at an unusually high rate.
Lagos began as a cluster of islands in a lagoon and now holds over 15 million people, growing by thousands every week.
